documentation.range: The distribution of Eunectes notaeus encompasses approximately 15 degrees in latitude through the Paraguay River basin, from the Pantanal region in Bolivia, Paraguay, and Brazil throughout the Wet Chaco, to northeastern Argentina, where it reaches the southernmost limit of its geographical range (Waller and Micucci 1993, Henderson et al. 1995, Dirksen 2002, Waller et al. 2007). Outside the Wet Chaco and Pantanal, the species marginally occurs in the Atlantic forest in wetlands and tributaries of the Paraná River near the border between Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay (Waller et al. 1995, Moura-Leite et al. 1996), and in some Pampas wetlands of Rio Grande do Sul, in Southern Brazil, where a reproductive population has been found (Santos et al. 2013). A few specimens have been recorded downstream the Uruguay River in Uruguay (Canavero et al. 2010, Moreira et al. 2018) but the existence of a resident population for this country still needs confirmation. The extent of occurrence (EOO) of E. notaeus was estimated in 400,000 km2 (Micucci et al. 2006). Our estimate was 450,000 km2. Assuming a conservative 1:3 wetland/dry land ratio throughout this wetland dominated area, we estimate that the total area of occupancy (AOO) for this species is not less than 150,000 km2.
documentation.population: Eunectes notaeus appears to be common throughout most of its range in Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina (including areas where harvesting is ongoing - T. Waller pers. obs.), but rare or occasional in Uruguay (Giraudo et al. 2012), where apart from a few records downstream the Uruguay River (Moreira et al. 2018), the existence of a resident population has not been substantiated yet. In the Brazilian Pantanal it was the second species (out of 22) in frequency, accounting for 15.1 per cent of all specimens found in a collection of snakes (Strüssmann and Sazima 1993, Strüssmann 1997). Embert (2007) categorized this species as common in his assessment of Bolivian reptiles. During the filling of the reservoir of Yacyretá dam, in the Paraná River at the border between Argentina and Paraguay, c. 1,500 individuals were rescued from the flooded islands (Waller et al. 2001). In a two days survey carried out by the authors in 2018 in the southernmost limit of the species' range in the province of Entre Rios, Argentina, 37 individuals of varied sizes were found along a short stretch of the Parana River (T. Waller, pers. obs.). The sustained harvest of an average of 3,500 skins of E. notaeus in a single wetland in northern Argentina during 18 years, without detrimental consequences for the species (Micucci et al. 2002/2019), suggests that this snake achieves high densities in suitable habitats. Micucci and Waller (2007), based on intensive sampling during daily hunting sessions in Northern Argentina, broadly suggested a density of 30–60 E. notaeus per km2. These estimates over an AOO of about 15 million ha, suggest that the total population would be in the order of the millions of individuals.
documentation.habitats:
The Yellow Anaconda is primarily found in the Wet Chaco and Pantanal (Giraudo et al. 2012), but it occurs marginally in Pampas (Santos et al. 2013) and Atlantic Rainforest (Waller et al. 1995). It occurs in aquatic inland ecosystems, specifically swamps, seasonally flooded marshes and riverine habitats, which are associated with the Paraguay River and middle sector of the Paraná and Uruguay Rivers (Strüssmann and Sazima 1993, Dirksen 2002, Santos et al. 2013). Most of this region is a poorly drained plain without major geographic features, however, some soil types represent barriers to its dispersal, confirming the role of watercourses and wetlands as routes for gene flow and distribution (McCartney-Melstad et al. 2012, Kershaw et al. 2013). Eunectes notaeus tolerates some anthropogenic disturbance, adapting well to artificial waterbodies, such as irrigation channels (T. Waller pers. obs.) and is frequently found in and around the Metropolitan area of Asunción (Paraguay), even in polluted waters (E. Buongermini and P. Cacciali, pers. obs.).

It is a semi-aquatic, viviparous and generalist species that feeds on a variety of vertebrates, mainly on birds and mammals but also on fishes, caimans and other snakes; this species also scavenges on dead fishes during droughts and takes eggs during birds’ nesting seasons (Strüssmann and Sazima 1991, Waller and Micucci 1993, Strüssmann 1997, Waller et al. 2007). It is an active forager that feeds frequently (Camera et al. 2019). Females eat more frequently than males. Diet varies between sexes but there is a high overlap. Larger individuals, mainly females, can include large preys in their diet, but continue to eat small prey (Miranda et al. 2016).

Eunectes notaeus are viviparous and mating in Argentina occurs from August to October, ovulation takes place during November, with parturition after 160–180 days, from March to April (Waller et al. 2007). A similar pattern has also been observed for the Brazilian Pantanal (C. Strüssmann, pers. obs.). Females in Argentina reproduce every two years in average, depending on fat reserves. This proportion can differ among years and among regions (Waller et al. 2007). According to the literature, E. notaeus produces 5–37 hatchlings per clutch (Dirksen 2002, Reed and Rodda, 2009). Based on a large sample from Northern Argentina, average clutch size was estimated in 24 new borns per event with a range of 7–65 (Waller et al. 2007). Growth appears to be relatively fast in wild populations, with males and females capable of doubling their size in the first year of age and reaching sexual maturity in the second or third year at about 1.3 m SVL for males and 1.5 m SVL for females (Waller et al. 2007).

No data available on longevity or survivorship of wild E. notaeus are available. Captive individuals can live for over 20 years, but longevity is expected to be significantly lower in the wild. Hatchlings are exposed to a variety of predators, however, the relatively large neonatal size, fast growth rates, and fierce temperament of this species, suggest that hatchlings and juveniles may be able to elude predation by outgrowing vulnerable offspring sizes in a few months (Waller et al. 2007).
documentation.threats: Current threats for this species include wetland habitat loss for agricultural expansion and intentional killings for skin, meat, oil, and retaliation for small livestock predation. Most of this species' range encompasses the major river basins in the Wet Chaco and Pantanal, where no large dams or large-scale wetland reclamation is ongoing (T. Waller pers. obs.) and habitat availability has remained very stable (Waller et al. 1995, 2007). A potential risk are the numerous hydroelectric power plants to be built around the Pantanal in the coming years; the hydrological cycle and the total inundated area every year may be impacted as well as the associated fauna (e.g. Campos et al. 2020). It should be noted, that the species also benefits from some man-made habitats, like artificial ponds and roadside channels (Waller et al. 2007), as well as vegetated dams or water reservoirs and rice fields (Santos et al. 2013, E. Buongermini pers. obs.). In Argentina, while harvesting may historically have had detrimental impacts prior to the establishment of a management plan, under the YAMP harvesting of this species has been restricted to the province of Formosa, where it is carried out under an adaptive management approach and, according to harvest monitoring reports (Micucci et al. 2002/2019, Waller et al. 2011), appears to have been sustainable over the last 18 years. There is no substantial harvesting elsewhere in South America. A small number of Yellow Anacondas are seasonally killed in the high-water season of the Brazilian Pantanal, in prevention or retaliation for small livestock predation in riverside communities (Fogaça, 2018).
documentation.measures: Listed in CITES Appendix II. Classified as Vulnerable in Argentina (Giraudo et al. 2012) and Least Concern in Paraguay (Motte et al. 2009; P. Cacciali pers. comm. 2020), Bolivia (Embert, 2007, Ministerio de Medio Ambiente y Agua 2009) and Brazil (Nogueira and Martins, 2018). It is a priority species for conservation in Uruguay (Carreira and Estrades 2013). Harvest in Argentina has been managed under a sustainable approach since year 2002 (Waller et al. 2011). Near 10% of the range of this species is included in protected areas from Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay. It would be advisable to establish whether or not there is a reproductive and viable population in Uruguay.
documentation.use_trade: This species was hunted for its skin throughout its range for half a century (Waller and Micucci 1993) until the late 1990s. Approximately 140,000 skins originated from stockpiles accumulated as a result of a hunting ban established by Argentina in 1986 were released for export between the years 1996 and 2000 under strict control of the national authorities (Micucci et al. 2006). International trade diminished after 2001 due to better CITES enforcement in range countries. Paraguay introduced a voluntary suspension of trade of all CITES Appendix II listed species in 2003, while Argentina implemented a sustainable harvest programme. As of 2002, the species started to be harvested in specific areas of the Province of Formosa, Argentina, under the Yellow Anaconda Management Program (YAMP) that has been producing 2,500 to 5,500 individuals per year (Micucci et al. 2006, Micucci and Waller 2007, Waller et al. 2011). From 2002, the YAMP became the main source of Yellow Anaconda skins entering international trade, with 62,324 skins exported by Argentina between 2002 and 2018 according to the CITES trade database. Paraguay exported 8,174 skins until 2013 (CITES trade database), when its stockpiles, obtained before the voluntary suspension established in 2003, were used up. Trade in wild live specimens for the pet market is negligible. Eunectes notaeus is occasionally collected for food or medicine by traditional communities from Brazil (Alvez et al. 2011), Bolivia (Embert 2007), Paraguay (Aquino-Shuster et al. 1991) and Argentina (Gallardo 1977).
documentation.rationale: Eunectes notaeus is listed as Least Concern. This species has a large range (450,000 sq. km) in relatively well-preserved wetlands in four different countries, trade is currently not a major concern for the species in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay. Localized impacts from land conversion for agricultural development may exist in Argentina, Paraguay, Bolivia and Brazil. A potential future threat are the numerous hydroelectric power plants to be built around the Pantanal in the coming years that may affect the hydrological cycle of that wetland.
